music_cards_circle_analysis_iivi_text: A minor chord a fourth below a dominant is its ii, and the dominant resolves to the I.
music_cards_circle_analysis_key_text: For each chord you name the key it belongs to and its job there, such as ii, V or I. The example is Fly Me to the Moon. It starts in C.
music_cards_circle_analysis_subs_text: A dominant a half step above the I it resolves to is a tritone sub, like Db7 to C. A dominant a whole step below is a backdoor, like Bb7 to C.
music_cards_circle_analysis_v_of_text: A dominant that resolves to a chord other than the home key's I is a secondary dominant, a V of. A minor chord before it is a related ii.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_four_text: Tap each to hear the borrowed chord, then C. Each one takes a note from C minor.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_parallel_tex: A major key and the minor key on the same tonic are parallels, C major and C minor. The minor has three more flats. Borrowed chords come from it into the major key.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_spot_text: A borrowed chord holds a note outside the major scale. Look for a flat 3, flat 6 or flat 7 over the tonic.
music_cards_circle_chords_any_text: Pick any key and the wedge moves with it. The chords change, the numerals don't.
music_cards_circle_chords_pattern_text: The seven chords of a major key always run {numerals}. In C they are {names}. Tap Next to hear them.
music_cards_circle_chords_pattern_title: One pattern in every major key
music_cards_circle_chords_wedge_text: I, IV and V are the key and its two neighbours. The minor chords ii, iii and vi are the relative minors of IV, V and I.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_one: {key} major has 1 flat, {flat}. There's no second-to-last, so learn it.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_step: {accidentals}. The second-to-last is {flat}, so the key is {key}.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_text: A flat key takes its name from the second-to-last flat. The exception is F, with 1 flat, which you have to learn.
music_cards_circle_count_round_text: Start at C, which has no sharps or flats. Each step clockwise adds one sharp. Tap Next to walk round.
music_cards_circle_count_sharp_step: {accidentals}. The last is {last}, a half step up is {key}.
music_cards_circle_count_sharp_text: The major key is a half step above the last sharp. Find the last sharp in the signature, then go up one half step.
music_cards_circle_key_has_none: {key} major has no sharps or flats.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_ccw_text: One step counter-clockwise is a fourth up and adds one flat (or removes one sharp).
music_cards_circle_neighbours_cw_text: One step clockwise is a fifth up and adds one sharp (or removes one flat). Tap Next to see three steps.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_rel_step: {major} major has {minor} minor as its relative.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_rel_text: The relative minor sits on the middle ring, 3 half steps below the major tonic. The key across the wheel is a tritone away.
music_cards_circle_order_counting_text: A key with N sharps uses the first N in the order. A key with N flats uses the first N flats.
music_cards_circle_order_flats_text: Flats use the same letters in reverse: {order}. Read the sharps sentence from the end and you have the flats. Tap Next to add them one at a time.
music_cards_circle_order_next: {note} is next. The signature now has {count}.
music_cards_circle_order_ready_text: Next, name the sharps or flats of a key, in order: {sharps} for sharps, {flats} for flats. Go as fast as you can stay right.
music_cards_circle_order_sharps_text: Sharps always join a key signature in the same order: {order}. Remember it as Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle. Tap Next to add them one at a time.
music_cards_circle_order_title: The order of sharps and flats
music_cards_circle_relative_share_none: {major} major and {minor} minor share no sharps or flats.
music_cards_circle_relative_text: Every major key shares its signature with a minor key 3 half steps below its tonic. Count down 3 half steps from the major tonic.
music_cards_circle_secondary_any_text: A secondary dominant is a dominant seventh a fifth above the chord it leads to. It's written V of, or V/ followed by the target.
music_cards_circle_secondary_find_step: {name}: the target is {target}, a fifth above is {root}, so {dom}.
music_cards_circle_secondary_find_text: Name the target chord and go up a fifth. Make that a major chord with a flat seventh, even when the target is minor: E7 before Am, not Em7.
music_cards_circle_secondary_four_text: Tap each to hear the dominant resolve to its target.
music_cards_circle_secondary_four_title: Four in the key of C
music_cards_circle_secondary_v_of_c: G7 is the V of C, a fifth above C.
music_cards_circle_secondary_v_of_v: {dom} is V/V: a fifth above G, leading to G.
music_cards_circle_signature_bass_text: In bass clef the same signature sits on different lines. The order of the sharps and flats stays the same.
music_cards_circle_signature_ready_text: You see a signature and name the key. Count first, then apply the rule for sharps or flats. Speed comes with practice.
music_cards_circle_signature_rule_sharp: {accidentals}, the last is {last}. A half step up gives {key}.
music_cards_circle_signature_rule_text: With sharps, the key is a half step above the last sharp. With flats, it's the second-to-last flat, and F has 1 flat.
music_cards_circle_signature_staff_text: A key signature sits at the start of every line, after the clef. Count the sharps or flats and you know the key. Tap Next to see some.
music_cards_circle_signature_staff_title: Sharps and flats on the staff
music_cards_circle_wheel_cw_text: Going clockwise from C the keys are {keys}. Each is a fifth above the last. Tap Next to walk round.
music_cards_circle_wheel_flat_text: On the other side the keys, read clockwise towards C, are {keys}. Counter-clockwise from C they run F, Bb, Eb, Ab, Db.
music_cards_circle_wheel_meet_text: At the bottom the sharp and flat names meet: B or Cb, F# or Gb, Db or C#. The wheel shows B, F# and Db.
music_cards_fb_differing: from the {lo} to the {hi} it is {value}
music_cards_fb_fifth_text: A 5th is 7 half steps: the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}. Tap Next to see each pair of strings.
music_cards_fb_fourth_text: A 4th is 5 half steps. Strings are usually tuned {common} frets apart, so a 4th is the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}.
music_cards_fb_half_text: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. One fret is one half step. A minor 3rd is 3, a major 3rd is 4, a 4th is 5, a 5th is 7 and an octave is 12.
music_cards_fb_high_g: The {names} string is tuned high, above the string next to it, so it sits apart from the rest.

match.countPlural=one: The irregular pair has a gap of {list} instead of {common}. A shape that crosses a smaller gap moves higher and a larger gap lower, by the difference. Tap Next to see the 5th across it.
match.countPlural=other: The irregular pairs have gaps of {list} instead of {common}. A shape that crosses a smaller gap moves higher and a larger gap lower, by the difference. Tap Next to see the 5th across each.

music_cards_fb_markers_guitar: The figure shows the dots at frets 3 and 5. Higher up there are dots at 7 and 9, and two at 12. Fret 12 is the open string's note an octave higher.
music_cards_fb_markers_ukulele: Ukuleles usually have dots at frets 5, 7, 10 and 12, with two at 12. They help you find your place. Fret 12 is the open string's note an octave higher.
music_cards_fb_match_step: Fret {fret} on the {lo} is the open {hi}.
music_cards_fb_naturals_text: The natural notes are A B C D E F G, then A again. There's a sharp between most of them, but not between B and C or between E and F. The {name} string below shows the naturals in its first five frets.
music_cards_fb_next_text: Fret {fret} on a string is the open note of the next string up in pitch.
music_cards_fb_next_text_reentrant: Fret {fret} on a string is the open note of the next string up, counting from the {from} and skipping the high {names} string.
music_cards_fb_oc_follows: When both gaps are {common} frets, the octave two strings up{notHigh} is {rel}.
music_cards_fb_oc_none: No two strings two apart here{notHigh} have both gaps of {common} frets.
music_cards_fb_octave_shapes_text: An octave is 12 half steps, which is 12 frets on one string.
music_cards_fb_open_text: The open strings are the notes you hear with no finger down. From string {count} to string 1 they are {notes}.
music_cards_fb_tap_next_pair: Tap Next to see each pair.
music_cards_fb_thirds_text: A major 3rd is 4 half steps: the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}. A minor 3rd is 3 half steps, always one fret lower than the major 3rd.
music_cards_tier1_groove_all_text: Here is one bar of the simplest groove, counted 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &, where & is the half beat. Tap Next to add the drums one at a time.
music_cards_tier1_groove_grid_text: In the drill, each drum is a row and each column is a count, and the picture shows the example filled in. Mark the squares where you heard a hit, then check. The levels go {levels}.
music_cards_tier1_groove_hat_text: The hi-hat keeps time with a steady run of hits. The first two levels play every eighth note, and the sixteenths and trap levels sometimes play every sixteenth.
music_cards_tier1_groove_kick_text: The kick is the low drum, and it lands on beat 1 of every bar in every groove here. The other kick hits move around from groove to groove. Tap Hear it for a kick on beats 1 and 3.
music_cards_tier1_groove_snare_text: The snare is the sharp crack on beats 2 and 4. The sixteenths level can add extra snare hits around it, and in trap the main snare moves to beat 3.
music_cards_tier1_home_cadence_text: Chords can lead away from home and back. Tap Next to hear one chord at a time.
music_cards_tier1_home_checked_text: The drill works out the key from the whole recording, so home belongs to the song and not to the stretch you looped. A minor key's home is its first note, and the relative key's tonic counts too, such as C and A. A song that changes key, or sits long away from home, can fool it.
music_cards_tier1_home_one_text: In most music one note feels like the place the music rests. That note is the tonic, or home, and the key is named for it: in {note} major home is {note}.
music_cards_tier1_home_recording_text: Listen for the note the music settles on, the one where it could stop. Play it on your instrument, sing it, or pick it from the notes below. The octave doesn't matter.
music_cards_tier1_home_resolve_text: A major scale climbs 1 to 7, then reaches 1 again. Tap Unresolved to stop on 7, then Resolved to step up home.
music_cards_tier1_home_step_3: It sounds unfinished and wants to go home.
music_cards_tier1_home_step_4: It sounds finished, because you're back home.
music_cards_tier1_idea_close: A 4-way close voicing puts a melody note on top with the next three chord tones close below it, all within an octave. The drill goes through a ii-V-I with each chord tone on top in turn. A major chord with its root on top takes the 6th instead of the 7th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_drop2: Drop-2 starts from the 4-way close voicing and drops its second voice from the top down an octave. That note goes in the left hand and the other three stay in the right. The chord spreads wider than the close voicing, with the same four notes.
music_cards_tier1_idea_evans: Bill Evans's spreads on a ii-V-I use three notes in the left hand and two in the right. The left hand plays the 3rd, 7th and 9th, and on the V the 7th, 3rd and 13th. The top right-hand note is the melody, with one voice under it.
music_cards_tier1_idea_garland: Red Garland's block chords on a 12-bar blues: the left hand plays the 3rd, 7th and 9th of the chord. The right hand plays the melody in octaves, with a note a 5th above the lower one between them. The drill gives one chord a bar.
music_cards_tier1_idea_locked: In George Shearing's locked hands the melody note is doubled an octave below in the left hand, with a 4-way close chord under it in the right. A melody note that belongs to the major 6th chord (root, 3rd, 5th or 6th) gets that chord. Any other melody note gets the diminished seventh chord.
music_cards_tier1_idea_monk: Thelonious Monk's shells on a 12-bar blues keep the root in the left hand. On the I the right hand plays the 3rd, b7 and root. On the IV and V it plays the 3rd and b7, with the root and b9 together on top, a half step apart.
music_cards_tier1_idea_quartal: A quartal stack is three notes a 4th apart, all in the left hand. The drill moves it up the dorian mode for two octaves. To stay in the mode, one of its 4ths is sometimes an augmented 4th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_quartal_tune: Every chord in a tune's changes gets a left-hand stack of two 4ths taken from the chord's scale, with one of the chord's guide tones inside it: the 3rd or 7th, the 4th on a sus chord, or the 6th on a sixth or diminished chord. A chord on a diminished scale, such as a b9 dominant or a diminished 7th, has no such stack, so it gets a tritone under a 4th. The picture shows the first chord.
music_cards_tier1_idea_sevenths: A seventh chord stacks the root, 3rd, 5th and 7th, all from the notes of the key. The chord on each degree gets its quality from the key: maj7 on the I and IV, m7 on the ii, iii and vi, 7 on the V and m7b5 on the vii. The drill plays them in root position, up the key and back.
music_cards_tier1_idea_slash_tune: Every chord in a tune's changes becomes a triad over its root, chosen by the chord type. A minor 7th, 7sus or dominant takes the major triad a whole step below the root. A major 7th takes the triad on its 5th, and a half-diminished chord the minor triad on its b3.
music_cards_tier1_idea_so_what: The So What chord is a stack of 4ths with a 3rd on top, all from the dorian mode. The two lowest notes go in the left hand and the other three in the right. To stay in the mode, a 4th can grow to an augmented 4th and the top 3rd can shrink to a minor 3rd.
music_cards_tier1_idea_sus: A 7sus chord voiced as a slash chord: the root and 5th in the left hand, and the major triad a whole step below the root in the right. For C7sus that triad is Bb major, written Bb/C. The right hand can use any inversion of the triad.
music_cards_tier1_idea_two_hand: A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass. In a ii-V-I the left hand plays the 3rd and 7th (the 7th and 3rd on the V), and the right hand adds the 9th, 5th and 13th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_upper: Each dominant in a tune gets a 1-3-7 shell in the left hand and a triad on top that adds colour tones. A b9 mark takes the VI triad (b9 13). Otherwise a dominant that resolves to a minor chord, or is marked alt, #9 or b13, takes the bVI triad (#9 b13), and any other takes the II triad (9 #11 13).
music_cards_tier1_pads_band_text: In this drill the band plays a loop and you play any pads and any rhythm over it. It's scored on time, meaning how close your hits sit to the sixteenth grid, and on keeping every bar going. A bar counts as kept going when it has at least two hits.
music_cards_tier1_pads_fill_text: The grid shows a groove bar, then a fill bar with the same hi-hat and the snare playing eighths on 3 and 4. Hear it adds the crash and kick on the next bar's one. In the drill, with A fill every 4 or 8 bars set, the fill bar needs more hits than your usual bar and a hit on the next bar's one.
music_cards_tier1_pads_space_text: You don't have to fill every beat. This bar is only the kick and snare, with no hi-hat, and it still counts as kept going. Only a bar with no hits, or one hit, loses that part of the score.
music_cards_tier1_pads_vary_text: Keep a groove going and change a little each time round. Tap Plain to hear one bar twice, or Varied to hear it then the same bar with one more kick on the & of 4. The grid shows the plain bar until you tap one.
music_cards_tier1_role_3: {name} is the 3rd, which makes the chord major.
music_cards_tier1_role_R: {name} is the root, the note the chord is named for.
music_cards_tier1_role_b3: {name} is the 3rd, which makes the chord minor.
music_cards_tier1_role_other: {name} is a tone of the chord.
music_cards_tier1_stack_add_left: Add {note}, {interval} above {below}, in the left hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_add_right: Add {note}, {interval} above {below}, in the right hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_start_left: Start on {note}, the lowest note, in the left hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_start_right: Start on {note}, the lowest note, in the right hand.
music_cards_tier1_stacked_text: Here is the first one the drill gives, {symbol}. Tap Next to add its notes from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_stacked_text_monk: Here is the first chord with a cluster, {symbol}. Tap Next to add its notes from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_tones_chord_text: Your answer should finish on a tone of the chord that's playing. {chord} is made of {names}, lit on the keys.
music_cards_tier1_tones_each_text: Tap Next to light the tones from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_tones_land_text: End your phrase on one of these tones and it sounds settled. Notes outside the chord are fine on the way there. The chord changes as the groove goes round, and the tones change with it.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_bite_text: Hold a note and pulse your bite by wiggling your jaw lightly on the mouthpiece, with no hard squeeze. The Aerophone sends the bite as pitch bend, and the drill reads those values. If it says no bite arrived, set the bite to send pitch bend (E-Wind bite mode gives vibrato).
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_checks_text: The drill listens for {seconds} seconds from your first note. You pass with the rate within {tolerance} percent of the target and an evenness of at least {evenness} percent. It shows how deep your pulses are but doesn't score that: aim for a small, even wobble around the note, not a slide between notes.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_hear_text: Each tap above alternates a note with the note a semitone below, one pair per pulse. The app can't bend a pitch, and real vibrato is much narrower than a semitone. So this shows the rate only, not the width.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_pulses_text: The drill sets a tempo and a number of pulses a beat, so {slowPulses} a beat at {slowBpm} is {slowRate} pulses a second. The top setting, {topPulses} a beat at {topBpm}, is {topRate} a second, the going rate from Larry Teal. Tap each rate to hear it.
